headline: Data-thin Thursday at Jones Inlet as primary buoys go dark mid-June
subhead: With 44025 offline and 44097 reporting intermittently, the bite read leans on seasonal pattern and shoreline signal rather than live SST.
body_markdown:
The analyst desk is running on fumes this morning. The 44025 sensor array — the workhorse reference twenty-odd miles south of Fire Island that normally anchors any honest Jones Inlet report — is offline, and 44097 out toward Block Island has been coughing up intermittent water-temperature returns. The most recent satellite SST package in the catalog is dated June 10, two days stale, and no fresh overnight intelligence was logged. That means no clean number to hang on the inside-versus-outside thermal gradient today, and any specific Fahrenheit figure you see floating around the docks this morning is somebody's guess, not measurement. What we do know is seasonal: by the second week of June the back of Hempstead Bay is typically running well into the mid-60s on the flood and pushing toward 70 on a sun-baked afternoon ebb, while the ocean side of Jones Inlet itself lags by several degrees as cleaner Atlantic water punches in on every incoming tide. That gradient is the engine, and it is almost certainly running right now whether or not the buoy is reporting it.

For this beat, a stalled data feed in mid-June doesn't change the playbook much — it just forces you to fish the structure you trust. The thermal break sits right inside the inlet throat, where warmer bay water meeting cooler ocean wash sets up a feeding line that bass and bluefish lean on hard during the back half of the outgoing. Fluke should be holding on the cleaner, cooler sand south and east of the inlet, with the Sloop Channel edge and the drifts south of the Meadowbrook holding the better class of fish on the incoming. Weakfish — and there are more of them in this bay than there have been in fifteen years — are a slack-tide and low-light story, sitting deep in the bay on the channel edges off Freeport and the Wantagh marshes.

The surf side has shifted into its early-summer rhythm. The big bunker pods that lit up Jones Beach in May have largely moved through, and what's left on the beach is a mixed bag — resident bass working sand eels and spearing at first light along the Field 6 cuts and the bar east of the inlet, with the better grade of fish caught on dropping water before sunrise. The bluefish presence inside the bay has firmed up over the past two weeks; the snapper class is showing as expected for the calendar, and the harbor blues in the 18-to-22-inch range are running the bait edges on the incoming around the bridges. On the fluke side, the drifts south of Jones Inlet have been holding fish but the ratio of shorts to keepers is what it always is in June — you'll work through a lot of 16- and 17-inch fish before you find a true doormat, and the better-class fish are coming off the cleaner ocean drifts in 30 to 50 feet rather than the bay drifts inside.

Bait pattern matches the water. Bucktails dressed with squid strips or Gulp continue to outproduce strictly natural baits on the fluke drift when the wind cooperates, and the soft-plastic shad-on-jighead presentation that took over the late-fall bass game last year is carrying right into the early summer pattern for bay bass holding around the Meadowbrook and Loop pilings. Live snappers, once they bulk up another inch, will be the move for bay blues and any bonus bass by late June.

Looking out three to five days, the controlling variable is wind. With no live offshore wave data to lean on, I'd watch the marine forecast more carefully than usual — a sustained southwest blow over 15 knots will stack warm surface water against the South Shore beaches and accelerate the bay warm-up, which pushes the fluke bite out of the back and concentrates it on the ocean drifts off Short Beach and east toward Gilgo. A clean northeast piece of weather, conversely, will flush cooler water into the inlet and trigger the better tide-line bite right in the throat on the outgoing. The new moon on the 14th sharpens current speed mid-week, which favors the bridge bite on the incoming and the inlet tide-line on the outgoing.

Fish the structure, fish the tide, and don't trust any temperature number you can't tie to a working sensor. The pattern is mid-June — the data just hasn't caught up to the calendar this morning.
